newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: PARER SAYS MINING JOBS WILL INCREASE
Federal Resources Minister, Warwick Parer, says increasing demands in Asia for Australian coal will see a boost in mining jobs during the next 10 years.
Senator Parer opened the third APEC Coal Flow Seminar, on the New South Wales Central Coast today.

He says industrialised economies are consuming electricity at an alarming rate, and coal's contribution to APEC's demand for power is expected to expand from 37-percent in 1992, to 42-percent in the year 2010.
Senator Parer says that during his recent trip to Japan and Korea, investors indicated they wanted to buy Australian coking coal, but wanted gurantees of supply.
He says buyers said they needed to take some equity in Australian coal mines to guarantee supply, whereas five or six years ago it was Australians looking for equity to gain markets.
HERRON SAYS ABORIGINAL PEOPLE MUST BE EMPOWERED
The Federal Aboriginal Affairs Minister says he's concerned about Aboriginal deaths in custody.
John Herron says state and federal governments have failed Aboriginal people by making them economically dependent.
But Senator Herron says there is a generational change in the mindset of Aboriginal people, the majority of whom are now under 25 years old.
He says governments should be helping these people by empowering them to take control of their own lives, and freeing them of their economic dependency on the state.
DODSON DOUBTS OVER BLACK DEATHS SUMMIT
Indigenous Social Justice Commissioner Mick Dodson says the Federal Government is rubbing salt into the wound by expecting ATSIC to pay for a national summit on black deaths in custody.
The Government announced the summit after a report by Mr Dodson yesterday showed black deaths in custody have increased since a Royal Commission in 1989.
Mr Dodson says it's disgraceful that Aboriginal people are now expected to pay for the ineptitude of the authorities in implementing the Royal Commission's recommendations.
He also told Triple J's Morning show the summit could turn into just another talkfest.
AMNESTY CONCERNED ABOUT AUSTRALIA HUMAN RIGHTS COMMITMENT
Amnesty International has called on Australia's Federal and State governments to act immediately to improve human rights in this country.
A Human Rights Commission report shows the rate of Aboriginal Deaths in Custody has increased since the 1989 Royal Commission.
Amnesty's spokesman on Australian matters, Heinz Schurmann-Zeggel, says the government calls Deaths in Custody a priority issue, but doesn't seem to be demonstrating any urgency in tackling it.
He says Amnesty is concerned there may be a wavering commitment to human rights in general, claiming there are other indicators for that.
KOALA CULLING BACK ON AGENDA
Culling koalas on South Australia's Kangaroo Island, is back on the agenda, with a taskforce saying that's the best way to solve over-population.
The taskforce says the options of relocation and sterilisation are more cruel and impractical, citing potential for starvation and ecological problems.
The taskforce recommends two-thousand of the more than five thousand koalas on Kangaroo Island should be killed in a one-off operation.
But, with the Government expected to make a decision before Christmas, State Environment Minister David Wotton has reiterated koalas won't be culled.
DEMOCRATS AND GREENS OPPOSE UNIVERSITY FEE RISES
Independent Senators Brian Harradine and Mal Colston will determine the fate of the Federal Government's planned university fee rises, with opposition parties lining up against the increases.
Democrats Senator, Natasha Stott-Despoja, says it would be unfair to impose up-front full cost fees on students and increase the Higher Education Contribution Scheme, or HECS, for new students.
The Australian Democrats and the ALP also intend opposing the moves in the Senate.
University Vice-Chancellors are urging the Senate to support the fee rises, because universities have already had their operating grants cut.
ROTHWELLS JURY RESUMES DELIBERATIONS
The jury in the Rothwells conspiracy trial will resume its deliberations in Perth later this morning, despite telling the judge it has so far been unable to agree on its verdicts.
The jury returned to court yesterday afternoon, after sending the presiding judge a note saying it was stuck on several points.
However Justice Kerry White urged the 12 jurors to put aside any personal feelings and continue their considerations.
Justice White said while he was able to discharge them, he would be reluctant to do so, adding that he was entitled to accept a majority verdict of at least ten.
The jury will be going into its fifth day of deliberations, in a trial that has so far lasted almost 14 months.
